OpenAI Moderation API Pricing: Free, Rate Limits, and Alternatives

OpenAI moderation models are free. See pricing, rate limits by usage tier, Python examples, and when an OpenAI-compatible alternative fits better.

OpenAI’s Moderation endpoint is free for OpenAI API users. To choose a production workflow, check the supported inputs and categories, your account’s rate limits, and how the endpoint fits your review process.

This guide separates the official pricing answer from the practical engineering decision.

TL;DR

  • OpenAI's Moderation endpoint is free for OpenAI API users, according to OpenAI's Help Center.
  • OpenAI's omni-moderation-latest model is designed to detect harmful content and accepts text and images as input, according to the official OpenAI model page.
  • Free pricing does not remove workflow costs such as logging, review queues, policy mapping, retries, fallback behavior, and application-specific decisions.
  • Choose OpenAI's free endpoint if you already use OpenAI directly and your moderation workflow fits its categories and response format.
  • Consider EvoLink Moderation 1.0 if you already use EvoLink and want multimodal checks, a risk summary and per-call billing in the same workflow.

Is the OpenAI Moderation API free?

Yes. OpenAI's official Help Center states that the Moderation endpoint is free for OpenAI API users and that usage of the tool does not count toward monthly usage limits.

Source: OpenAI Help Center: Is the Moderation endpoint free to use?

That is the pricing answer. The next question is operational:

Is a free moderation endpoint enough for your production workflow?

For prototypes, internal tools, and simple text-first moderation, it may be. For applications that handle user-generated content, image uploads, AI agents, or review queues, the API call is only one part of the system.

What does OpenAI moderation cover?

OpenAI documents omni-moderation-latest as a moderation model designed to identify potentially harmful content in text and images. The official model page describes it as OpenAI's most capable moderation model and lists support for text input/output and image input. Source: OpenAI model page for omni-moderation-latest OpenAI's moderation guide also explains content classification categories and notes that some categories are text-only. If you send only images to omni-moderation-latest, categories that do not support image inputs return a score of 0. Source: OpenAI Moderation guide

That means teams should read the category table carefully before assuming that every text category maps directly to image moderation.

The real cost is workflow, not just API pricing

The Moderation endpoint may be free, but a production moderation system still needs decisions around:

  • where to run checks: before model calls, after model responses, or both
  • how to map categories to allow, review, or block decisions
  • how to log moderation outcomes without storing sensitive content unnecessarily
  • how to handle false positives and appeals
  • how to moderate image uploads separately from text input
  • how to monitor latency, errors, and rate limits
  • how to keep policy behavior consistent across product surfaces

Those are engineering and operations costs. They do not show up on a pricing page, but they decide whether the moderation layer is actually maintainable.

In a typical workflow, check prompts before sending them to the model and check outputs before delivery. Send uncertain results to review, keep a minimal record of decisions, and plan for retries and appeals.

When OpenAI's free endpoint is a good fit

OpenAI's free Moderation endpoint is often a good first choice when:

  • you already use OpenAI directly
  • your app is mostly text-first
  • you only need OpenAI's documented moderation categories
  • you can build your own review and escalation workflow
  • your team is comfortable owning response parsing, thresholds, and logs

In that case, the free endpoint is hard to argue against. Start there, test it against your real content, and measure false positives and missed cases before routing production traffic.

When an OpenAI-compatible alternative makes sense

EvoLink Moderation 1.0 is a paid alternative with an OpenAI-compatible /v1/moderations route. EvoLink accepts at most one image per request.

  • text-only, image-only, and text-plus-image checks through one endpoint
  • 13 harm categories with per-category scores
  • an evolink_summary object with risk_level, flagged, violations, max_score and max_category
  • flat per-call pricing instead of token math
  • a response shape that is easier to map to allow, review, or block logic

How to use OpenAI Moderation API in Python

If you are already using the OpenAI SDK, a basic text moderation call looks like this:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()

response = client.moderations.create(
    model="omni-moderation-latest",
    input="user text here"
)

print(response.results[0].flagged)
print(response.results[0].categories)

For EvoLink, set EVOLINK_API_KEY to your EvoLink key and EVOLINK_BASE_URL to the HTTPS API base ending in /v1 from your EvoLink API configuration. The response includes the additional evolink_summary object.

import os

from openai import OpenAI

# EVOLINK_API_KEY=YOUR_EVOLINK_API_KEY
client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["EVOLINK_API_KEY"],
    base_url=os.environ["EVOLINK_BASE_URL"],
)

response = client.moderations.create(
    model="evolink-moderation-1.0",
    input=[{"type": "text", "text": "user text here"}],
)

summary = response.model_extra["evolink_summary"]
print(summary["risk_level"])
print(summary["violations"])

OpenAI vs EvoLink for pricing and workflow

Criterion OpenAI Moderation API EvoLink Moderation 1.0
Billing Free for OpenAI API users Paid at a flat rate per call
Main endpoint shape /v1/moderations OpenAI-compatible /v1/moderations
Text moderation Supported Supported
Image moderation Supported by omni-moderation-latest, with category-specific input support Supported for image-only and text-plus-image requests
Fields for policy decisions Interpret flagged, categories and category_scores in results Use evolink_summary.risk_level and violations alongside category scores
Best fit Teams already calling OpenAI directly Teams integrating moderation into an existing EvoLink workflow

Practical recommendation

Use OpenAI's free Moderation endpoint if your application is already OpenAI-native and your moderation policy maps cleanly to its documented categories.

If your team already uses EvoLink, evaluate its per-call cost and use evolink_summary.risk_level as one input to your application’s allow, review or block rules.

Use a multi-layered moderation system if your application has custom policy requirements that need brand rules, human review, appeals, or compliance workflows beyond any single moderation API.

FAQ

Is the OpenAI Moderation API free?

Yes. OpenAI's Help Center says the Moderation endpoint is free for OpenAI API users and does not count toward monthly usage limits.

Does OpenAI moderation support images?

Yes, omni-moderation-latest accepts images as input according to OpenAI's official model page. However, OpenAI's moderation guide notes that some categories are text-only, so teams should review category-level input support before relying on image-only moderation.

Is EvoLink Moderation cheaper than OpenAI Moderation?

OpenAI’s Moderation endpoint is free for OpenAI API users. EvoLink charges a flat rate per call. Compare the cost of the complete workflow, including review and maintenance.

Can I use EvoLink as an OpenAI Moderation API alternative?

Yes. Use your EvoLink API key and the model evolink-moderation-1.0 on EvoLink’s compatible /v1/moderations route. Update your response handling to account for EvoLink’s separate evolink_summary object.

Should I moderate prompts, outputs, or both?

For production AI applications, many teams moderate both inputs and outputs. Input moderation can reduce unsafe requests before they reach a model. Output moderation can catch unsafe generated responses before they reach users.

What is omni-moderation-latest?

It is OpenAI’s moderation model for text and images. Read flagged, categories and category_scores in results and apply your own moderation policy.

What is the OpenAI Moderation API rate limit?

Free access describes billing. Request and token limits still apply. In the model reference, RPM means requests per minute, RPD means requests per day where listed, and TPM means tokens per minute.

OpenAI Moderation API rate limits vary by account tier and can change over time. Check the OpenAI rate limits documentation and your account's usage limits page before planning production throughput.

How do I use the OpenAI Moderation API in Python?

Install the openai package, set OPENAI_API_KEY, and call client.moderations.create() with the model omni-moderation-latest and your text. For images, pass input as an array of objects. Each image item has type: "image_url" and an image_url object containing url, as shown in the OpenAI API reference linked below.

item.title: The real cost of LLM inference is the GPU you are not using
item.content:encoded:
The real cost of LLM inference is the GPU you are not using

Two historical API rates for input tokens differed 600-fold. See how GPU utilization, idle rental hours and peak rates shape LLM inference costs.

A 2026 study (arXiv:2603.28576, §4) compared two API price benchmarks. The study used USD 60 per million input tokens for its 2020 GPT-3 benchmark and USD 0.10 for the economy-tier Gemini 2.0 Flash in February 2025, a 600-fold difference. It estimated a price half-life of 1.1 years for its economy tier.

What the deflation headlines hide is the part that actually sets your bill: how many of your GPU hours are doing useful work. Inference is billed by the token, but served by the hour.

A data centre aisle of GPU servers, most glowing with activity while one sits dark and idle

The number teams miss

A June 2026 vLLM benchmark (arXiv:2606.11690, §§4–5) ran Mixtral 8x7B Instruct in FP16 on two H100 NVL GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=2). It used a combined rental rate of USD 13.96 per hour and synthetic requests of 512 input tokens and 256 output tokens, with prefix caching disabled. The table divides the GPU rental cost by measured output-token volume over the same period. Request rates count arrivals offered to the server.

Mixtral 8x7B on two H100 NVL GPUs Effective cost per 1M output tokens
1 request per second (near idle) about $15.25
100 offered requests per second (near saturation) about $0.87

The two measurements differ by 17.5×. At 25 offered requests per second, the cost was about USD 0.95 per million output tokens. At 100 offered requests per second, the server completed about 17.4 requests per second. The study found costs from USD 0.21 to USD 15.25 per million output tokens across six H100 configurations and the measured loads. Treat those values as measurements for this test workload. In production, measure throughput at a load that meets your latency target.

For the same hourly rental rate, operating at 40% of peak output throughput raises the cost per output token by a factor of 2.5. In the following examples, utilization is the share of peak output throughput that the service actually achieves. A GPU can report high activity while producing few output tokens.

This is why two teams running the same model can quote wildly different unit costs. One runs a bursty chatbot at 40 percent utilization; the other runs a saturated batch pipeline at 90 percent. The model, the hardware, and the sticker price are identical. The unit cost is not. When a vendor quotes you a cost per token, ask what utilization assumption is baked into it.

Open-weight models made this worse

A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model uses a subset of its weights for each token. Mixtral 8x7B activates about 12.9 billion parameters per token and contains 46.7 billion in total. For an all-on-GPU deployment, budget memory for all the weights at their stored precision, plus the KV cache and runtime overhead. Active parameters help estimate compute per token. Memory bandwidth, expert routing and batch size also affect throughput.

Estimate the break-even point for your own workload. Compare the API bill for the same mix of input and output tokens with the cost of renting GPUs for the hours you need, including idle hours, and operating the service. Measure output throughput under your traffic pattern and latency target. API prices, model configuration and utilization all affect the result.

The second hidden cost: time of day

As of 25 November 2026, the direct DeepSeek API applies peak rates from 01:00 to 04:00 and from 06:00 to 10:00 UTC, Monday through Friday except on Chinese public holidays. Free and low-cost LLMs for coding and writing in mid-2026

A mid-2026 comparison of free tiers, budget APIs and local models for coding and writing, with examples of when to use a stronger model.

Lightweight and heavy AI model cost balance on a dark editorial field

Most of the work you ask a language model to do does not require the most expensive frontier SKU. Boilerplate code, first drafts, summarization, rewrite passes, test generation, and ticket triage are volume problems. A budget model can handle routine work, with a stronger model for the tasks that need it.

This guide ranks free and cheap options for coding and writing as of mid-2026, explains trade-offs, and shows when to promote a task to higher-tier models.

What “cheap” means here

Tier Rough definition Examples (names evolve)
Free $0 list or generous free quota Gemini Flash free tiers, open weights self-host, some gateway free SKUs
Budget API Typically well under frontier list rates DeepSeek V4 Flash, mini/Haiku/Flash lines, GLM Turbo, MiniMax mid tiers
Local cheap Your electricity + GPU, $0 tokens Qwen-Coder / DeepSeek quant on 12–24GB VRAM
False economy Cheap tokens, expensive human cleanup Tiny models on hard multi-file refactors

Cheap is total cost of quality, not $/1M tokens alone.

Best cheap LLMs for coding (2026)

DeepSeek V4 Flash / V4 Pro (API value)

  • Use for: Bulk codegen, unit tests, refactors with CI as the judge, internal agents.
  • Why cheap wins: Near-frontier coding for many tasks at aggressive unit economics.
  • Watch: Hardest agentic SWE tasks may still favor frontier models.

Gemini 3.5 Flash / 2.5 Flash

  • Use for: Fast iteration, large-context “read the monorepo and explain,” multimodal tickets.
  • Why: Flash pricing + enormous context changes how you prompt (paste more, guess less).
  • Watch: Validate agent pass rates on your harness; speed ≠ SWE crown.

GPT mini / nano class (5.4 mini, etc.)

  • Use for: IDE autocomplete-style tasks, small functions, structured transforms.
  • Why: Strong tooling ecosystem, predictable APIs.
  • Watch: Escalate multi-file architectural work.

Claude Haiku 4.5 and small Sonnet tiers

  • Use for: Clean code style, careful small diffs, docstrings, review comments.
  • Why: Anthropic quality curve often holds better than peers at small sizes for prose-heavy code review.
  • Watch: Not a replacement for higher-tier models on gnarly repo repair.

Qwen coder line (open / API)

  • Use for: Local and self-host coding, bilingual teams, fine-tunes.
  • Why: Best-in-class open coder culture; excellent 4-bit local fits.
  • Watch: You own ops, evals, and update cadence.

GLM-5.x Turbo / Flash, MiniMax M2.x/M3 mid tiers

  • Use for: Regional deployments, bilingual product engineering, long-context budget coding.
  • Why: Competitive open/API value charts in 2026.

Kimi K2.7 Code / K2 free-class SKUs

  • Use for: Code-specialized work and long-context engineering without K3 prices.
  • Why: Moonshot’s coding SKUs target exactly this band; K3 sits higher for max intelligence.

ByteDance Seed 1.6 Flash / 2.0 Mini

  • Use for: Latency-sensitive product features and mid-size coding tasks.

Grok smaller / efficient modes (when offered)

  • Use for: General coding under a cost ceiling with strong reasoning-per-dollar.

Local quantized coders (the truly cheap path)

On a 24GB GPU, a ~27–32B Q4 coder is the practical “always on” brain. Rules:

  • Name the quant (Q4_K_M vs Q5).
  • Reserve VRAM for KV cache or you will OOM mid-file.
  • Use local for private code; still run CI.

Best cheap LLMs for writing (2026)

Writing quality is not coding quality. Rank writing models on instruction following, tone control, factual restraint, and edit quality.

Job Budget pick Escalate to
Blog outline / first draft Gemini Flash, GPT mini, DeepSeek Flash Claude Sonnet-class models for final polish
Rewrite for clarity Haiku / Flash / mini Sonnet-class for executive tone
Long report synthesis Long-context Flash or Kimi mid Higher-tier models with citations
Marketing variants Cheap models in batch Human editor always
Policy-sensitive copy Do not use free random gateways Grounded + reviewed stack

Rule: Cheap models draft; humans or stronger models ship. For claims that can harm users, apply a hallucination team checklist.

Free options that are actually usable

  1. Self-host open weights (Qwen, DeepSeek, Llama, GLM builds) — free tokens, not free time.
  2. Vendor free tiers — great for prototypes; terrible as a sole production dependency.
  3. Gateway free SKUs — read rate limits and data retention.
  4. Student / startup credits — real money, temporary.

Free is perfect for learning and demos. Production should assume free tiers disappear on a Friday.

Recommended stacks

Indie hacker / solo dev

  • Daily coding: DeepSeek Flash or Gemini Flash
  • Local private: Qwen-Coder quantized
  • Hard bugs: weekend budget for one frontier model
  • Writing: Flash draft → human edit

Startup eng team

  • Default PR assistant: budget API coder
  • Security-sensitive modules: frontier + second-model review
  • Docs: cheap long-context model with RAG
  • Eval: golden tasks weekly

Enterprise pilot

  • Data residency first, then price
  • Cheap models only behind logging and DLP
  • High-risk writing (customer, legal) needs grounding + approval

When cheap models fail (pay up)

Escalate when you see:

  • Multi-file architectural refactors with subtle invariants
  • Security, crypto, auth, payments
  • Ambiguous product decisions framed as “just write the RFC”
  • Repeated CI failures that a senior engineer would solve by reading design history

A $0.05 failure that burns two engineer-hours is not cheap.

Multi-model thrift: the smart middle

You do not need five frontier models. You need diversity on hard calls:

  1. Generate with a budget model.
  2. On high-risk outputs, review with a different family.
  3. Keep the transcript.

That pattern is cheaper than generating everything on the top SKU and safer than trusting one free model.

FAQ

Best free is usually a local open coder you control (Qwen-coder class quantized) or a vendor free tier for non-sensitive work. For quality-per-hour, a few dollars of DeepSeek/Gemini Flash often beats fighting rate limits.

Can free models replace Claude or GPT for production?

For bulk tasks, often yes. For your hardest 5% of engineering work, usually no. Measure with a golden set.

In mid-2026, some Kimi SKUs appeared in free tiers or on gateways; K3 is a higher-end intelligence model. Check current Moonshot listings.

ChatGPT API: How to Set Up, Pricing, and Code Examples (2026)

A practical guide to setting up the ChatGPT API, comparing models and pricing, and building applications with code examples.

The ChatGPT API gives developers programmatic access to OpenAI models. This guide covers API key setup, model selection, pricing, code examples, and practices for building applications and managing costs.

What Is the ChatGPT API?

The ChatGPT API lets developers integrate AI capabilities into applications through HTTP requests. Applications send structured requests to OpenAI and receive JSON responses containing model output.

How the ChatGPT API Works

The process follows four steps:

You send a request. Your application sends a POST request to OpenAI with a JSON payload containing a model name, messages, and parameters such as temperature and token limits.

OpenAI processes the request. The model generates a response and returns it in a JSON object. With streaming enabled, tokens arrive incrementally.

Your application receives the response. The response includes generated content, token usage, model information, and a request ID.

Billing occurs. Charges depend on processed tokens. Input and output tokens may have different rates.

Prompt length, model selection, and caching affect performance and cost.

ChatGPT API Models and Pricing (2026)

Model availability, features, and prices can change. Check OpenAI’s API pricing and developer documentation for current details. Pricing is generally based on input and output tokens, which may have different rates.

Models and Capabilities

The source lists GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4 mini, GPT-5.4 nano, GPT-5.4 pro, GPT-5.2, GPT-5 mini, GPT-5 nano, GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1 mini, GPT-4.1 nano, o3, o4-mini, and o3-mini. Its specific claims about launch dates, prices, context windows, model availability, and capabilities are time-sensitive and should be checked against current official documentation before use.

How to Choose a Model

Choose a model based on your task, quality requirements, latency, and budget. Test candidates on representative workloads and compare output quality and cost.

  • Customer support, Q&A, and content generation: compare models on representative requests.
  • Code generation, analysis, and agent workflows: evaluate quality on your own tasks.
  • Image understanding and multimodal applications: confirm the model’s supported inputs.
  • Math and multi-step reasoning: test reasoning models against your requirements.
  • Classification and extraction: consider throughput and cost alongside accuracy.

How to Set Up the ChatGPT API

You need an API key to authenticate requests. Treat it as a secret and store it securely.

How to Obtain an OpenAI API Key

Step 1: Access the OpenAI Platform

  • Visit platform.openai.com/api-keys and sign in or create an account.

Step 2: Create Your API Key

  • Open API Keys in the dashboard.
  • Select Create new secret key and optionally give it a project-specific name.
  • Copy the key when it is displayed; it may not be shown again.

Step 3: Store It Securely

  • Store the key in a password manager or environment variable.
  • Never commit API keys to version control or expose them in client-side code.
  • If you use a .env file, add it to .gitignore and keep the file out of version control.

Security notes:

  • A key can grant access associated with your account and billing.
  • If a key is lost, create a replacement.
  • Revoke keys that may have been compromised.
  • Use separate, appropriately scoped keys for different projects when available.

Setting Up Your Development Environment

The API can be used from any programming language that can make HTTP requests. Python, JavaScript, and Java are common choices.

1. Python: Simplicity and a Rich Ecosystem

Python’s syntax and library ecosystem make it a common choice. OpenAI’s Python package can simplify authentication, request formatting, and error handling. Packages such as python-dotenv can help manage environment variables.

Python is also used in machine learning, data science, web development, and automation, making it useful for projects that combine API calls with data processing.

2. JavaScript: Flexibility for Web Applications

JavaScript works for backend applications with Node.js and for web applications using frameworks such as React, Vue, or Next.js. Its asynchronous features, including async/await and Promises, support non-blocking API requests.

3. Java: Scalability and Performance

Java is commonly used for enterprise applications. Static typing can catch some errors at compile time, and its concurrency features can help applications handle multiple requests. It can suit software that integrates with existing Java systems.

The examples below use Python. If you use JavaScript or Java, adapt the syntax to your language and SDK.

Best Practices for Using the ChatGPT API

1. Write Clear and Specific Prompts

Clear, specific instructions can improve the usefulness of responses.

  • Specify the desired format, tone, and length.
  • Provide examples when useful.
  • Use developer instructions to set behavior and context.
  • Break complex tasks into smaller steps.

Example:

prompt.py

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()  # Reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment.

# Vague instructions leave the topic and format open.
vague = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write about marketing."}],
)
print(vague.choices[0].message.content)

# Specify the audience, deliverable, and focus.
specific = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",
    messages=[
        {"role": "developer", "content": "Write concise advice for SaaS teams."},
        {"role": "user", "content": (
            "Write three paragraphs on email marketing for a SaaS startup "
            "selling to small businesses. Cover deliverability, segmentation, "
            "and automation."
        )},
    ],
)
print(specific.choices[0].message.content)

2. Use Structured Outputs for Reliable Data

For JSON or other structured data, use the API’s structured output features instead of parsing free-form text. Check the documentation for the supported format and constraints.

prompt.py

import json

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": (
        "Extract the product name, price in US dollars, and category: "
        "The iPhone 15 Pro costs $999 and is a smartphone."
    )}],
    response_format={
        "type": "json_schema",
        "json_schema": {
            "name": "product_extraction",
            "strict": True,
            "schema": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "product_name": {"type": "string"},
                    "price": {"type": "number"},
                    "category": {"type": "string"},
                },
                "required": ["product_name", "price", "category"],
                "additionalProperties": False,
            },
        },
    },
)
choice = response.choices[0]
message = choice.message
if message.refusal:
    raise RuntimeError(message.refusal)
if choice.finish_reason != "stop" or not message.content:
    raise RuntimeError(f"No complete JSON response ({choice.finish_reason}).")
product = json.loads(message.content)
print(product)

3. Implement Streaming for Better User Experience

Streaming can show response content as it arrives rather than waiting for the complete response.

prompt.py

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()
with client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain quantum computing simply."}],
    stream=True,
) as stream:
    for chunk in stream:
        if chunk.choices:
            text = chunk.choices[0].delta.content
            if text:
                print(text, end="", flush=True)
print()

4. Manage Context and Token Limits

A model’s context window limits the tokens available for input and output. Monitor usage to avoid truncation and unexpected costs.

  • Keep conversation history concise; summarize or trim older messages.
  • Use the appropriate output limit supported by the model and API.
  • Check response usage information.
  • Consider chunking or summarizing long documents.

prompt.py

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain an API in two sentences."}],
    max_completion_tokens=500,
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
if response.usage is not None:
    print(f"Tokens used: {response.usage.total_tokens}")

5. Handle Errors Gracefully

Requests may fail because of network issues, rate limits, invalid input, or service outages. Handle errors according to the SDK and API documentation.

prompt.py

from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
import math
import random
import time

from openai import APIConnectionError, APIStatusError, OpenAI, RateLimitError


def retry_delay(error, attempt):
    hint = error.response.headers.get("Retry-After")
    if hint:
        try:
            seconds = float(hint)
        except ValueError:
            try:
                date = parsedate_to_datetime(hint)
                seconds = max(0.0, (date - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds())
            except (ValueError, TypeError, OverflowError):
                seconds = -1
        if math.isfinite(seconds) and seconds >= 0:
            return seconds
    return 2**attempt + random.uniform(0, 0.25)


client = OpenAI(max_retries=0, timeout=10.0)
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Suggest one way to improve API reliability."}]
max_attempts = 3
for attempt in range(max_attempts):
    try:
        response = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4.1-mini", messages=messages)
        print(response.choices[0].message.content)
        break
    except RateLimitError as error:
        # Retry transient rate limits. Quota and billing errors need action.
        if error.code != "rate_limit_exceeded" or attempt == max_attempts - 1:
            raise
        delay = retry_delay(error, attempt)
        if delay > 5:
            raise
        time.sleep(delay)
    except APIConnectionError as error:
        raise SystemExit("Connection failed. Check connectivity before resending.") from error
    except APIStatusError as error:
        raise SystemExit(f"API returned HTTP {error.status_code}.") from error

6. Optimize Costs

  • Choose a model suited to the task and compare quality and cost.
  • Set an output limit to avoid unnecessarily long responses.
  • Cache results for repeated queries where appropriate.
  • Batch similar requests when supported and suitable.
  • Monitor spending in the OpenAI usage dashboard.

prompt.py

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()
prompt = "Summarize in one sentence: The meeting moved from Monday to Tuesday."
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    max_completion_tokens=150,
    temperature=0.3,
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Consult the OpenAI pricing page for current model prices.

7. Implement Rate Limiting

Rate limits may apply to requests and tokens over time, depending on account and service conditions. A 429 response indicates a rate-limit condition.

  • Use backoff when appropriate.
  • Track request rates and throttle if needed.
  • Check your account’s current limits and eligibility for changes.
  • Consider batch processing for suitable workloads.

8. Use Function Calling for Tool Integration

Function calling allows a model to request that your application call a function or tool. Your application handles the call and returns results as appropriate.

prompt.py

import json

from openai import OpenAI


def celsius_to_fahrenheit(celsius):
    return celsius * 9 / 5 + 32


client = OpenAI()
tools = [{
    "type": "function",
    "function": {
        "name": "celsius_to_fahrenheit",
        "description": "Convert a temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit.",
        "strict": True,
        "parameters": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"celsius": {"type": "number"}},
            "required": ["celsius"],
            "additionalProperties": False,
        },
    },
}]
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Convert 20 degrees Celsius to Fahrenheit."}]
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1", messages=messages, tools=tools,
    tool_choice="required", parallel_tool_calls=False,
)
assistant = response.choices[0].message
if not assistant.tool_calls:
    raise RuntimeError(assistant.refusal or "The model did not request the tool.")
messages.append(assistant)
for call in assistant.tool_calls:
    if call.function.name != "celsius_to_fahrenheit":
        raise ValueError(f"Unexpected tool: {call.function.name}")
    arguments = json.loads(call.function.arguments)
    fahrenheit = celsius_to_fahrenheit(**arguments)
    messages.append({
        "role": "tool",
        "tool_call_id": call.id,
        "content": json.dumps({"fahrenheit": fahrenheit}),
    })

final = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4.1", messages=messages)
print(final.choices[0].message.content)

9. Secure Your API Key

  • Never commit keys to version control.
  • Keep keys in environment variables or another secure store.
  • Rotate keys when needed and revoke old or exposed keys.
  • Use separate keys per project where available.
  • Monitor usage for unexpected activity.
  • Restrict key permissions where supported.

10. Test with Different Models

Compare models on representative workloads for quality, latency, and cost. Start with a model that meets your requirements and move to another if testing shows a need.

Rate Limits and Access Tiers

Limits and account tiers can change. Check the OpenAI usage dashboard and current documentation for account-specific limits, spending controls, and rate-limit details. When a request is rate-limited, follow the API’s guidance and use an appropriate backoff strategy.

App Ideas to Build with the ChatGPT API

1. Customer Support Chatbots

Build assistants that answer FAQs, track orders, troubleshoot issues, and provide customer support. Function calling can connect an application to CRM, ticketing, or order-management systems.

2. Virtual Assistants for Productivity

Build assistants that manage schedules, draft emails, organize tasks, summarize documents, and extract action items from meeting notes using productivity APIs.

5. Data Analysis and Insights

Let users query databases in natural language, generate reports, identify trends, and create explanations of data. Validate outputs against the underlying data.

6. Code Generation and Debugging

7. Knowledge Bases and Intelligent Search

Yes. OpenAI provides an API for programmatic access to models. Applications can make HTTP requests or use official SDKs; check current documentation for available models and features.

What each tool is

Zapier is a no-code automation platform for connecting apps without writing code. It offers more than 7,000 app integrations, a visual interface, and pricing based on task volume.

n8n is an open-source workflow automation tool with a visual editor. It can be self-hosted or used through n8n Cloud. It supports code execution inside workflows, branching logic, AI agent nodes, and custom integrations through HTTP requests or JavaScript.

Cost

Zapier pricing scales with task count. At 2,000 tasks per month on the Starter plan, the source lists a price of $29.99 per month. At 100,000 tasks per month on the Teams plan, it lists $103.50 per month. Costs can rise for high-volume workflows such as CRM syncing, bulk email processing, and lead routing.

n8n Cloud starts at $24 per month for 2,500 workflow executions, according to the source. Self-hosting is another option: the source estimates that running n8n on a $6-per-month VPS can make hosting costs relatively fixed. Actual costs depend on the server and workload.

Flexibility and what you can build

Zapier is quick to set up for simple workflows, such as a trigger followed by an action. Two-step automations between popular apps can take minutes. More complex workflows may be limited by branching and error-handling options, and custom logic can require workarounds.

n8n supports multi-branch workflows, conditional logic, looping through arrays, JavaScript in workflow nodes, API requests with control over headers and authentication, reusable sub-workflows, and AI agent nodes. These features can support more complex automation, though they may require more technical setup.

AI capabilities

n8n includes AI agent nodes for incorporating LLM calls into workflows. The source describes chaining AI steps, adding tool-calling capabilities, and creating workflows with human approval steps. For example, a workflow could classify an email, query a CRM, draft a reply, and wait for approval before sending it.

Zapier also offers AI features. The source characterizes them as suitable for tasks such as reformatting text or generating summaries, and says they offer less flexibility for building multi-step agentic workflows with custom LLM calls and memory.

Where Zapier may be a better fit

Zapier is accessible and quick to set up. For small businesses automating simple tasks, such as sending email notifications to Slack or adding form submissions to a CRM, it may not require developer support. Its integrations and documentation can also help non-technical users get started.

For simple, low-volume automations between popular apps, Zapier may be a suitable choice. More complex requirements can make the choice less straightforward.

Which one is right for your business

  • Use Zapier if you need simple app-to-app automations, prefer a no-code setup, want to get started quickly, and have low task volumes.
  • Use n8n if you need complex multi-step logic, want to build AI-powered workflows, run high task volumes, prefer self-hosting and data control, or are building automations for a client or enterprise context.
  • Consider an n8n agency if you need n8n workflows but do not have in-house developers to build and maintain them.

Choosing for a growing business

The source argues that many businesses outgrow Zapier and later migrate to n8n. Such a migration can require rebuilding workflows. If you expect your automation needs to grow, consider the potential migration effort when choosing a tool.

On the other hand, if you are not technical and will not have someone manage n8n, Zapier's ease of use may justify its higher cost. The right choice depends on which tool your team can maintain and use effectively.

Is n8n really free?

n8n is open-source and can be self-hosted without a software subscription. You still pay for the server; the source estimates a basic VPS at $5–10 per month. n8n Cloud, the hosted version, starts at $24 per month, according to the source. Total costs depend on your setup and usage.

Is n8n harder to use than Zapier?

n8n has a steeper learning curve. Its visual editor supports complex workflows, which can take time to learn. Many non-technical users may find Zapier easier. For business-critical automation, consider whether you have the expertise to build and maintain n8n workflows.

Can n8n replace Zapier completely?

n8n may cover many business automation use cases, but the fit depends on the apps and integrations you need. Zapier has a larger selection of pre-built integrations, while n8n's HTTP request node and credential system can connect to APIs without a native integration. Check the required services and setup before deciding.

Top 5 small language models for production (practical guide)

A practical guide to five small language models for production, with selection criteria, deployment tradeoffs, tuning notes, and operational considerations.

Small language models here means models roughly 7 billion parameters or smaller that teams can run at reasonable cost on GPU inference or, with quantization, on a CPU. The goal is reliable, predictable behavior in production: low latency, a small memory footprint, and useful instruction following. This shortlist focuses on models that are straightforward to deploy, have an active ecosystem for quantization, runtimes, and fine-tuning, and can support retrieval-augmented generation, chat assistants, and lightweight agents.

Selection criteria

  • Inference efficiency: memory use and latency for batches of 1–8 tokens on common GPUs.
  • Instruction quality: out-of-the-box instruction following or availability of instruction-tuned weights.
  • Deployment ecosystem: support for ggml, ONNX, TensorRT, or popular libraries such as Transformers and llama.cpp.
  • Practical tradeoffs: failure modes, safety tuning, and maintenance costs. Choose based on latency targets, scale, and licensing constraints.

1. Llama 2 7B

Llama 2 7B is a pragmatic starting point for teams seeking a general-purpose model with broad ecosystem support. It can run on a single consumer GPU and has instruction-tuned variants and community fine-tunes, along with tooling for quantization and low-latency inference. It has limitations on complex reasoning, so production deployments should include safeguards against hallucinations.

Verdict: A general-purpose baseline for teams that need a widely supported model.

2. Mistral 7B Instruct

Mistral 7B Instruct is an option for instruction-following tasks where inference efficiency matters. Consider how it handles long, multi-step reasoning in your own workload, as a larger model may perform better on those tasks.

Verdict: Consider it when instruction quality relative to compute is a priority.

3. Falcon 7B

Falcon 7B is an option for services where throughput and token generation speed matter. Prompt format can affect its output, so prompt templates and few-shot examples may help improve consistency.

Verdict: Consider it for services with high-throughput and consistent-latency requirements.

4. MPT-7B-Instruct

MPT-7B-Instruct is an option for workflows that need longer context or streaming. It can be integrated into long-document workflows and custom context management. Evaluate instruction following and streaming behavior against your own requirements.

Verdict: Consider it for document-heavy use cases and streaming APIs.

5. StableLM / StableLM-Tuned-Alpha 7B

StableLM 7B and its tuned variants are options for teams that prefer a self-hosted stack over commercial endpoints. Evaluate their performance on classification, summarization, and retrieval augmentation, as well as whether additional tuning is needed for your use case.

Verdict: Consider it when control over the model and deployment stack is a priority.

Practical tradeoffs and tuning notes

  • Quantization and inference: These models can benefit from 4-bit or 8-bit quantization for CPU or lower-memory GPU deployments. Aggressive quantization can reduce quality; evaluate it on representative inputs.
  • Instruction tuning: Instruction-tuned variants can reduce prompt-engineering effort. If using a base model, consider preparing a small, curated instruction-tuning dataset to improve reliability before production.
  • Safety and hallucination: Small models can produce inaccurate answers. Add retrieval-based grounding, abstention rules, and post-generation filters for factual tasks.
  • Latency versus quality: If sub-50 ms token latency is a hard requirement, prioritize models with suitable runtime support and quantization. If quality matters more than latency, consider a larger model or an external API for demanding queries.
  • Licensing and compliance: Model terms vary and can change. Verify commercial-use rights, data-use clauses, and export controls for the chosen model before deployment.

Bottom line

Small models can offer an attractive cost and latency profile for production tasks, alongside limitations in reasoning and factuality. Llama 2 7B, Mistral 7B Instruct, Falcon 7B, MPT-7B-Instruct, and StableLM each present different deployment considerations. The right choice depends on latency targets, safety requirements, workload, and licensing constraints.

  • Test end to end with your retrieval and safety pipelines, not only on isolated benchmarks.

item.content:encoded:
AI content moderation: how it works, types, and the best APIs

Learn the main content moderation approaches, how automated systems fit into review workflows, and what to measure when evaluating them.

Content moderation used to be a text problem. Someone posted something, a classifier scored it, a human reviewed the borderline cases, and the queue mostly kept up. Then platforms got audio and video, and the queue stopped keeping up. A 45-minute podcast, a live stream, a voice agent conversation, a user-uploaded video — none of them can be scanned by a text classifier until something turns the speech into text first. And the volume is not close to reviewable by hand. That's the problem AI content moderation exists to solve, and the reason the interesting engineering has moved from "is this string toxic?" to "what's actually being said across ten thousand hours of audio, and which ninety seconds does a human need to look at?" This post covers what AI content moderation is, the six types you'll be asked about, how automated and hybrid systems actually work, which APIs are worth evaluating, and — the part most guides skip — how to measure whether yours is any good.

What is AI content moderation?

AI content moderation is the use of machine learning models to automatically detect, classify, and act on content that violates a platform's policies or legal obligations, across text, images, video, and audio. The "AI" part is doing specific work in that sentence. Rule-based moderation — banned word lists, regex patterns, hash matching — is still in production everywhere and still useful, but it can't read context. A model can tell the difference between a slur used as an attack and the same word quoted in a news report; a word list cannot. That contextual judgment is what separates AI content moderation from filtering.

Content moderation meaning, in practice

Strip out the vendor language and content moderation means three operations:

  1. Detect — find content that might violate policy.
  2. Classify — say which policy, and how severely.
  3. Act — remove, age-gate, demonetize, flag for human review, or do nothing. Most moderation failures are failures of step three, not step one. Teams build a detector, wire it straight to an automatic takedown, and discover that a 5% false positive rate on a large platform means thousands of wrongly removed posts per day — plus an appeals backlog nobody staffed for. The useful mental model: a moderation system's job isn't to make decisions. It's to route decisions to the right place, most of which is automated, some of which is human, and a small tail of which is a policy question nobody has answered yet.

6 types of AI content moderation

These six show up in every serious moderation architecture. Most platforms run three or four of them simultaneously, applied to different content tiers.

1. Pre-moderation

Content is reviewed before it goes live. Nothing publishes until it clears. This is the safest option and the slowest, so it survives where the cost of a miss is catastrophic and the volume is low: children's platforms, healthcare communities, regulated financial content, dating profile photos. The friction is real — users notice a publish delay — which is why pre-moderation usually applies to a subset of content types rather than everything.

2. Post-moderation

Content publishes immediately and gets reviewed after, usually within minutes. Violations come down once detected. This is the default for most social and UGC platforms. It preserves the real-time feel users expect and accepts a short exposure window as the cost. The engineering question is how short that window actually is, which for audio and video depends entirely on how fast you can transcribe.

3. Reactive moderation

Nothing is reviewed until a user reports it. The community is the detector. Cheap, scalable, and structurally biased — reactive moderation systematically under-catches violations in small communities, in languages the majority of users don't speak, and in any content that harms people who aren't there to report it. Nobody runs this alone anymore, but it remains a valuable signal layer on top of automated detection because human reports surface the things models were never trained to look for.

4. Distributed or community moderation

Trusted users, volunteer moderators, or reputation-weighted voting make the call. Think subreddit moderators or community notes. It scales well culturally, because the people applying norms are the people who hold them, and it scales badly legally — a volunteer isn't a compliance program. It works best as a layer inside a larger system rather than as the system.

5. Automated moderation

Models do the detection and, for high-confidence cases, the enforcement. This is the layer this post is mostly about. Automated moderation covers text classification, image and video classification, hash matching for known-bad media, and — increasingly — audio. The audio path is the one most teams haven't built: speech-to-text converts the spoken content into text, then content safety models classify it by topic and severity, and entity detection plus PII redaction handle the privacy side.

6. Hybrid moderation

Models triage; humans decide the hard cases. This is what mature platforms actually run, and it's less a distinct type than the correct assembly of the other five. The design question in hybrid moderation is where the threshold sits. Set it too aggressively and your human queue fills with obvious non-violations; set it too loosely and violations slip through automated approval. Getting that threshold right is an ongoing measurement exercise, not a launch decision — which is why the accuracy section below matters more than the API comparison. Moderate Audio and Video at Scale Turn spoken content into classified, reviewable text with content safety detection built in. Start free and test it on your own media.

How automated content moderation works

Under the hood, an automated moderation pipeline has four stages. Understanding them is the difference between buying a moderation API and building a moderation system. Stage one: ingest and normalize. Content arrives in whatever format users produce — a JPEG, an MP4, a 30-second voice note, a two-hour live stream. Normalization means getting each modality into something a model can score. For audio and video, that means speech-to-text first. This stage is where most latency lives and where most accuracy is lost, because everything downstream reads the transcript, not the audio. Stage two: classify. One or more models score the normalized content against a policy taxonomy — hate speech, harassment, self-harm, violence, sexual content, weapons, drugs, gambling, and so on — each with a confidence score. Good taxonomies are hierarchical, so you can enforce differently on "violence" in a news clip than in a threat. Stage three: decide. Scores hit a policy engine that applies thresholds, content-type rules, user reputation, and jurisdiction. This is the layer teams most often underbuild. A single global threshold is almost never right: the bar for a comment on a kids' app and a comment on a gaming forum are different bars, and they should be different numbers in config, not different models. Stage four: act and record. Enforcement plus an audit trail. The audit trail is not optional if you operate in the EU, and it's what makes appeals tractable. Store the score, the model version, the threshold that applied, and the resulting action.

Why audio is the hard modality

Text moderation gets the content for free. Audio moderation has to earn it, and everything the automatic speech recognition layer gets wrong propagates. Three failure modes show up repeatedly: Missed negations and short words. Drop "not" from "I'm not going to hurt you" and you've manufactured a threat. Short function words are exactly what a weaker model drops in noisy audio. Entity errors. Names, places, and numbers carry most of the meaning in a violation report. A model that garbles a named target turns a harassment case into an unmatchable string. Speaker confusion. In a multi-speaker recording, moderation without reliable speaker diarization can't tell you who said the thing. For a livestream with a host and callers, or a voice agent conversation, that's the entire question. The practical consequence: the accuracy of your audio moderation is capped by the accuracy of your transcription, and no amount of classifier tuning raises that ceiling. Teams that discover this late usually discover it during an incident review.

How to measure moderation accuracy at scale

This is the section that separates teams who improve from teams who ship a dashboard and hope. Stop using overall accuracy. On any real platform, the vast majority of content is fine, so a model that approves everything scores 97% accurate and is worthless. Use precision and recall per policy category, and track them separately. Set the threshold from the cost asymmetry, not from the F1 score. For child safety content, a false negative is catastrophic and a false positive costs a reviewer 30 seconds — bias hard toward recall. For a political speech category, a false positive is a public relations incident — bias toward precision. These are different numbers and they belong in config, reviewed quarterly. Build a gold set and keep it fresh. A few thousand items, labeled by humans against your actual policy, refreshed continuously as your content mix shifts. Without it you cannot tell whether a model update helped. With it, evaluation becomes a one-hour job instead of a quarter-long argument. Measure the transcript separately from the classifier. This is the audio-specific step nearly everyone skips. When a violation escapes, determine whether the speech model missed the words or the classifier missed the meaning. They demand completely different fixes — better transcription configuration versus threshold or taxonomy work — and if you don't separate them you'll spend months tuning the wrong layer. The techniques in how to evaluate speech recognition models apply directly here. Track reviewer agreement. If two human reviewers disagree on 20% of your queue, no model can hit 95% precision against that label set — the ceiling is your policy's ambiguity, not the model's capability. Low inter-rater agreement is a policy bug reported as a model bug. Watch the appeal overturn rate. It's the cleanest real-world precision signal you have, because it's produced by the people most motivated to find your false positives.

Frequently asked questions

What is AI content moderation?

AI content moderation is the use of machine learning models to automatically detect, classify, and act on content that breaks a platform's policies or legal obligations, across text, images, video, and audio. Unlike rule-based filtering, which matches banned words or hashes, AI moderation evaluates context — so it can distinguish a slur used as an attack from the same word quoted in a news report. Most production systems pair automated classification with human review of borderline cases.

What is the meaning of content moderation?

Content moderation means reviewing user-generated content against a set of rules and deciding what happens to it: publish, remove, age-gate, demonetize, or send to a human. It covers three operations — detect, classify, and act — and applies to every modality a platform accepts. The classification step is where AI does the most work today; the acting step is where most platforms make the most mistakes, because a single global threshold rarely fits every content type.

What are the 6 types of content moderation?

The six types are pre-moderation (review before publishing), post-moderation (publish first, review immediately after), reactive moderation (review only on user report), distributed or community moderation (trusted users decide), automated moderation (models detect and enforce), and hybrid moderation (models triage, humans decide the hard cases). Most mature platforms run several at once, applying different types to different content tiers and risk levels.

Can a speech-to-text API detect profanity and unsafe content in audio?

Yes. AssemblyAI says it returns content safety labels, profanity filtering, entity detection across 50+ types, topic classification, and PII redaction in text and audio as part of the same transcription request through its Guardrails and Speech Understanding API. Labels come back with timestamps, so a reviewer is sent to the 90 seconds that matter rather than a 50-minute file. The same capabilities run on live audio over the streaming WebSocket for real-time moderation.

What is the best content moderation API?

It depends on the modality you actually need to cover. Text-only platforms are well served by dedicated text moderation endpoints; visual platforms need image and video classification; general safety platforms bundle both with policy tooling. For audio and video platforms, the deciding factor is whether the vendor owns the transcription as well as the classification — classifying someone else's transcript gives you two accuracy problems and no way to debug an escape end to end.

How do you measure whether content moderation is working?

Track precision and recall per policy category rather than overall accuracy, which is meaningless when most content is compliant. Maintain a human-labeled gold set that refreshes as your content mix changes, set thresholds from the cost asymmetry between false positives and false negatives in each category, and watch your appeal overturn rate as a real-world precision signal. For audio, always measure the transcript separately from the classifier — a missed violation caused by a transcription error needs a completely different fix.

item.title: What is AI Inference? A Complete Guide
item.content:encoded:
What is AI Inference? A Complete Guide

AI inference is the runtime phase in which a trained model produces outputs from new inputs. It is the layer that shapes the cost, latency, and reliability of AI-powered products in production.

AI inference is the process by which a trained machine learning model produces an output in response to new input. When a chatbot answers a question, a search system returns a ranked result, or an image model generates a picture, inference is the step that turns a saved set of model weights into the response the user sees. Training builds the model; inference runs it whenever someone uses it.

Every chatbot reply, AI code completion, and AI-generated search summary requires inference. A model's training run happens once, while inference runs for each user request. As a result, the cost, latency, and reliability of the serving layer matter to the economics of AI-powered products.

What inference actually means

Inference is the runtime execution of a trained model with fixed weights. During training, the model's weights change as it learns from examples. After training, those weights are saved. Inference takes those fixed weights, combines them with a new input, and computes an output. The model itself does not change during inference; it performs a read-only forward computation.

For large language models, a single inference request has four stages, each with its own cost and latency profile:

  1. Tokenization. The input text is split into tokens—units roughly the size of a syllable or short word—that the model's vocabulary represents numerically. A 500-word document may become between 600 and 800 tokens, depending on the tokenizer. Tokenization affects the number of tokens processed per request.
  2. Prefill. The tokens pass through the model's layers in a single forward pass, producing a representation of the input and the first output token. This stage is compute-bound and highly parallelizable.
  3. Autoregressive decode. The model generates each subsequent output token one at a time, with each new token conditioned on the previous tokens. This stage is memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound, which helps explain its role in latency for long responses.
  4. Detokenization. The output tokens are converted back into the visible text the user receives.

Prefill is fast and parallel; decode is slower and sequential. This difference is one reason LLM inference has developed infrastructure specializations distinct from traditional machine-learning model serving. It also helps explain inference performance: time to first token is affected by prefill, while tokens per second is affected by decode. The two respond to different optimizations.

Inference vs training: the short version

Training and inference differ in many operational dimensions. Training consumes a large dataset and produces a set of weights; inference repeatedly consumes an input and produces an output.

Dimension Training Inference
Frequency Once per model version Once per user request
Duration Days to months Milliseconds to seconds
Hardware Tightly coupled GPU clusters with high inter-node bandwidth Individual GPUs or small groups
Cost shape Capital-like, paid upfront Operating-like, proportional to usage
Who absorbs the cost Model creator Application team
Optimization priority Model quality Cost, latency, reliability

For teams building on foundation models, training economics are often handled by the model provider, while application teams manage inference economics. Decisions about provider, deployment location, batching, caching, and fallback all affect inference.

Types of inference workloads

The definition covers any case where a trained model produces an output, but workload profiles vary enough that it is useful to name the main categories separately.

Text generation (chat). A common inference workload. A prompt enters, tokens are generated one at a time, and the response may be streamed to the user.

Reasoning and chain-of-thought. A variant of text generation in which a model produces a block of internal reasoning before its visible response. Examples include OpenAI's o-series, Anthropic's extended thinking modes, and DeepSeek-R1.

Embeddings. A text input produces a fixed-length vector rather than generated text. Embeddings are used for search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), clustering, and deduplication. Embedding inference supports many modern search and memory systems.

Vision and multimodal. An image, video frame, or audio clip combined with text produces a text or structured output. Latency can scale with input resolution, and cost depends on how many tokens the input decodes to. The same serving infrastructure can handle these workloads, but tokenization can be more expensive than for plain text.

Batch inference. For pipelines that do not require real-time responses—such as overnight enrichment, offline evaluation, or scheduled data preparation—batch inference can reduce costs.

Where inference actually runs

Running inference at production quality depends on three infrastructure layers that are not visible from the API surface but affect costs.

The GPU tier. Modern LLMs require GPUs with high memory capacity and bandwidth. NVIDIA H100 and H200 cards are used for large models. Smaller models can run on A100 or L40S cards, and very small models on consumer cards. The card choice affects throughput and the minimum model size that can be served without sharding across multiple cards. GPU memory sizing is a key part of planning LLM inference.

The serving engine. Raw GPU access is not sufficient. Efficient model serving requires an engine—also called an inference engine or inference server—to manage the KV cache, batch concurrent requests, and optimize memory layout. Commonly used engines include vLLM (open source, general purpose), TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA-specific, high performance), and SGLang (open source, optimized for structured generation). The serving engine can significantly affect throughput on the same hardware.

Regional deployment. Compute time is a major contributor to inference latency, and network round trips add further delay. For user-facing workloads, serving from a region close to the user can affect perceived responsiveness.

Operating this stack can suit teams with significant scale and dedicated infrastructure engineering. Others may purchase infrastructure, making the choice of purchasing model important.

How teams access inference in practice

Three patterns cover many production inference setups.

Self-hosting on rented GPUs. The team rents GPU capacity, deploys an open-weight model on a serving engine, and operates the full stack. This gives the team control and can be economical at very high volume, but requires infrastructure expertise in areas such as KV cache tuning, autoscaling, failover, and observability.

Direct provider APIs. The team calls a single provider's API. The provider handles the infrastructure. This is a fast path to a working product and a common way to start. The tradeoff is concentration risk and dependence on one pricing structure. Each request's cost, latency, and reliability depend on that provider's service.

Unified inference platforms. The team calls a single API that routes requests to multiple underlying providers and may include fallback, observability, and cost controls. This can retain the speed-to-ship advantage of direct provider APIs while reducing single-provider concentration risk and enabling workload-aware routing, such as using a lower-cost model for simple queries and a more capable model for complex ones.

Access pattern Speed to ship Operational burden Economical at Concentration risk
Self-hosted on rented GPUs Slow High (full infrastructure stack) Very high volume None
Direct provider API Fast Low Low to medium volume High (single provider)
Unified inference platform Fast Low Any volume, mixed workloads Lower (multiple providers)

The choice among these patterns depends on scale, engineering capacity, and how much variation in provider cost and reliability the team is willing to manage directly.

Why inference is the ongoing cost center

Inference affects the economics of AI-powered products because its cost scales with usage. A model's training cost is fixed and paid once by the provider or the team that trains it. Each inference request consumes additional compute. Ten users generate ten inferences; one million users generate one million. In practice, the unit economics of an AI product depend on the unit economics of inference.

This structure has two consequences. First, the cost of an AI feature grows with its usage: a feature with low adoption has a small inference bill, while one with high adoption has a larger one. Second, architectural choices that change inference cost compound as usage grows. These choices include model selection, prompt design, caching strategy, provider choice, and retry policy. A 20% reduction in per-request cost reduces marginal cost by the same proportion as usage grows.

The headline cost-per-million-token figure describes a particular request scenario; production workloads may differ from that scenario.

What most inference guides leave out

The mechanics above are well documented. Some operational considerations become clear when inference is run across providers in production:

  • The cheapest model is rarely the cheapest system. A model with a lower per-token price that fails more often, needs longer prompts to reach the same quality, or causes more retries can cost more per completed task than a nominally pricier model. Effective cost depends on the whole request path, so cost optimization involves architecture as well as price lists.
  • Output length is a strong lever. Because decode affects both inference latency and output cost, prompt changes that shorten responses can improve both.
  • Fallback policy affects price. Providers can have outages and rate limits. Whether a system fails, queues, or reroutes during those periods is an economic decision. Fallback chains affect availability and cost.
  • The ground can shift silently. Providers may change prices, quantize deployments, or swap model versions behind stable names. An inference setup tuned once and never rechecked can degrade over time.
  • Benchmark rank does not decide what serves a request. Leaderboards can help identify capable models, but choosing among them for a specific request also requires considering cost, latency, and availability constraints.

These considerations are not part of the definition of inference, but they can strongly affect production costs.

The question inference leads to

Understanding inference is a starting point. Production decisions include which model should handle each request, on which provider, at what price, and with what fallback. Choosing one fixed model makes those decisions once for all future traffic. Another approach is to treat model selection as a per-request decision, based on the request's needs.

For teams mapping workloads to models, model selection involves weighing the workload's requirements against model capabilities and costs.

LLM inference cost: what drives it and how to lower it

Understand the main factors behind LLM inference costs and practical ways to manage token use, model choice, context, and infrastructure.

LLM inference is a trained model doing its job at runtime: turning your prompt into a response, token by token, on expensive accelerator hardware. Training builds the model once. Inference runs it forever, on every request, for every user.

Forever is the operative word for a budget. Training is a one-time capital event you read about in headlines. Inference cost is an operating expense that scales with success: more users, more features, more agents, more spend. A successful product’s cumulative inference bill laps its training bill and never looks back.

The meter is the token, roughly three quarters of an English word. All inference pricing reduces to per-million-token rates, quoted separately for input (your prompt and context) and output (what the model generates). The cost per token is tiny. The volume never is. Every dollar you will ever spend on inference is arithmetic on that meter.

What does LLM inference cost per token actually mean?

LLM inference cost per token is not one number. For any model it is at least four numbers, and the spread between them is where production bills are decided:

Standard input versus output rates

As above, output runs about 5x input. Cap max tokens per use case and instruct models toward brevity. Small percentage, every call, forever.

Reasoning tokens

Models that think before answering bill the thinking as output, the expensive kind, and the user never sees it. If your bill jumped without a usage jump, check whether a default quietly flipped to a reasoning mode. Sometimes the depth earns its cost. Often nobody checked.

What drives LLM inference cost up?

Five drivers, ordered by how often they explain a shocking invoice:

  1. Unbounded output. Verbose defaults, unset max token limits, and reasoning modes left on for easy tasks all inflate the expensive side of the meter. Nobody approves this spend because it arrives one wordy answer at a time, which is exactly why it compounds unwatched.

How do you reduce LLM inference cost?

LLM cost optimization comes down to eight levers. Ranked by effort against savings:

  1. Route on cost, latency, and quality together. Good routers score all three; quality-only routing is how budgets die. Even a two-tier router, cheap model first with escalation on low confidence, captures most of the value and is a weekend of engineering.

  2. Impose output discipline. Max token caps per use case, concise-answer instructions, and no paying output rates for pleasantries.

  3. Measure per feature before optimizing anything. The uncomfortable one. None of the seven levers above can be aimed without knowing which product, feature, or customer generates the spend. LLM inference optimization without allocation is guessing with confidence, and it reliably tunes the visible chatbot while the background pipeline burns 80% of the budget.

Should you self-host to cut inference costs?

Only if you can keep the hardware busy. Self-hosting trades a per-token meter for a per-hour one, and the entire business case lives in utilization. Sustained, predictable, high-volume traffic on a busy cluster beats API rates decisively. Spiky or modest traffic on idle GPUs loses to the API every time, and you inherit an ops team as a consolation prize.

Then benchmark honestly: published LLM inference benchmark data measures tokens per second per GPU under your actual batch sizes and context lengths, and it is the difference between a plan and a hope. The AI inference economics here reward the boring answer. If volume is uncertain or engineering appetite is thin, stay on APIs and spend the energy on the eight levers above.

How do you track LLM inference cost to the product level?

Start from the question no provider dashboard answers: which feature, team, or customer generated this spend, and was it worth it? API consoles report totals by key. Totals do not survive contact with a CFO who wants the margin impact of the new AI feature, in numbers, by Thursday.

Getting to answers takes three layers. Tag usage by feature and environment so consumption has an owner. Normalize across providers into one view, because multi-model stacks are the norm and every vendor reports differently. Then allocate to unit economics: inference spend per feature, per customer, per transaction, the denominators the business actually runs on.
